submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires retrospectively when the current token is the element projected by the preceding 1-3 tokens: the identifier after a keyword (SELECT name), the copula or verb after a subject (x is, defendant pleaded, bank raised), the noun after a determiner (The cat, the triangle), the preposition after a localizing verb (sits on), or the onset digit or unit of a projected number frame (year 1600, range(10, 5 p.m., at sea, habite à). The same surface token fires weakly when the projecting left context is broken, and firing is unaffected by tokens after the peak, which rules out pure token identity and lookahead.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: When I finally decided to cross the border by train instead of flying, I had no idea how slowly the hours would pass. The carriage smelled faintly of coffee and old leather, and rain streaked the windows as we pulled away from the station just after dawn. I shared a compartment with an elderly woman knitting something blue, a student asleep against his backpack, and a conductor who checked our tickets twice and apologized both times. Outside, flat fields gave way to rolling hills, hills to dark forests, and forests to small grey towns with church towers, shuttered bakeries, and empty squares. At each stop new passengers climbed aboard with baskets, umbrellas, dogs, newspapers, and crying infants, while others waved goodbye from platforms and vanished into mist. A vendor moved through the aisles selling sandwiches wrapped in wax paper, hot tea in paper cups, chocolate bars, postcards of mountain lakes, and little wooden toys I had never seen before. I bought bread and cheese and ate slowly, watching raindrops race each other down the glass. Somewhere past noon the clouds broke and sunlight flooded the valley, turning wet meadows silver and making every puddle shine. Children ran alongside the tracks waving, sheep scattered across high pastures, and distant snowcaps appeared above a ridge of pine. We crossed a long iron bridge over a wide brown river where barges waited in line, and for a while the tracks ran beside a canal lined with poplars, locks, swans, and fishermen sitting motionless under dripping trees. The woman opposite me offered half her apple, told me about her grandchildren, and fell asleep mid-sentence with the knitting still in her lap. At the border, officials stamped passports without looking up, and two sleepy dogs sniffed our luggage before settling back under a bench. By evening the train slowed beside a harbor where gulls circled trawlers unloading the day's catch, and lights from waterfront cafes trembled on dark water. I found a small room above a bakery, woke before sunrise to the smell of warm bread, and spent the whole morning wandering narrow streets full of cats, laundry lines, shouting merchants, and doorways spilling music. In the afternoon I met an old school friend for coffee near the port, and over our second cup she mentioned that mon cousin habite à Marseille depuis le printemps dernier.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long travel narrative from a different genre burying the French 'habite à' frame deep in context, which the hypothesis says should still fire.
